option_c: It records the exact versions of all dependencies for reproducibility
option_d: It generates the browsable documentation website for the package
explanation: §30.2 describes `NAMESPACE` as an auto-generated file that tells R which functions are available to a user of `library(heormodel)` versus which are purely internal helpers, which is what prevents an internal helper like `clean()` from clashing with a `clean()` function from an entirely different package.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: In the `roxygen2` worked example for `run_markov_model()` in §30.3, what specific consequence follows from omitting the `@export` tag on a function the author intended users to call?
option_a: The function is automatically deleted from the `R/` folder
option_b: The function remains an internal helper, invisible outside the package -- a common cause of "but it worked when I ran the script directly" confusion
option_c: `devtools::check()` will refuse to run until the tag is added
option_d: The function's documentation is rendered in red text on the `pkgdown` site
explanation: §30.3's terminology box states that `@export` tells `roxygen2` a function should be listed in `NAMESPACE` as user-available; functions without it remain internal helpers invisible outside the package, which is called out as a common source of confusion after packaging.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: In the `targets` pipeline example of §30.4 (raw_data -> clean_data -> calibrated_params -> psa_results -> ceac_plot), what does the "pipeline / dependency graph" concept formally capture?
option_a: The physical order in which R scripts are saved on disk
option_b: The set of computational steps needed to go from raw inputs to final results, together with which steps depend on the outputs of others
option_c: A record of which collaborator last edited each function
option_d: The list of CRAN mirrors used to download package dependencies
explanation: §30.4 defines a pipeline as the set of computational steps from raw inputs to final results plus the fact that some steps depend on others' outputs (e.g., PSA depends on calibrated parameters, which depend on cleaned data) -- `targets` builds this dependency graph explicitly from the code rather than leaving it implicit in script run order.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: Per the build cache / memoisation example in §30.4, if a labelling typo in the CEAC plot code is fixed and `tar_make()` is re-run, what happens to the 10,000-simulation PSA step?
option_a: It automatically reruns because any change to the pipeline file triggers a full rebuild
option_b: It is skipped and its previously stored result is reused, because its own inputs have not changed
option_c: It reruns with a reduced number of simulations to save time
option_d: `targets` deletes the cached PSA result to force fresh validation
explanation: §30.4 explains that `targets`' build cache (memoisation) stores a step's result and reuses it as long as nothing it depends on has changed; fixing a labelling typo in the downstream CEAC plot code means only `ceac_plot` reruns, while the ten-thousand-simulation `psa_results` target is reused unchanged.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: Per §30.5, what is continuous integration (CI) as applied to an R-based health-economic model package?
option_a: A manual checklist a reviewer completes once before a submission deadline
option_b: The practice of automatically building and testing code every time it changes, without relying on a person to remember to run the checks
option_c: A method for calibrating transition probabilities automatically
option_d: A licensing framework for open-source R packages
explanation: §30.5 defines CI as automatically building and testing code every time it changes -- in the HEOR context, every push to GitHub triggers a robot that installs R and dependencies, runs the test suite and `R CMD check`, and reports pass or fail without the author needing to remember to do it.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: Per §30.5, what is a YAML workflow file used for in the context of GitHub Actions CI for an R package?
option_a: It stores the model's probabilistic sensitivity analysis results
option_b: It is a plain-text configuration file telling GitHub Actions what sequence of steps to run and when to run them (e.g., on every push)
option_c: It is the compiled output of `devtools::check()`
option_d: It replaces the `DESCRIPTION` file for package metadata
explanation: §30.5 describes YAML as a human-readable structured configuration format, and a "workflow file" as a YAML file telling GitHub Actions what sequence of steps to run (install R, install packages, run checks) and when (every push, only on main, nightly, etc.).

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: Per §30.6, why does the chapter recommend pointing an ERG reviewer at a tagged release rather than the live repository's default `main` branch view?
option_a: Tagged releases load faster on GitHub's servers than the default branch view
option_b: A tagged release is a fixed snapshot that does not change after the fact, so the model a reviewer received, reviewed, and cited in their report are provably the same artifact -- whereas `main` shows whatever changes have been pushed up to that moment
option_c: GitHub does not allow read-only collaborator access to the default branch
option_d: Tagged releases automatically include a `pkgdown` documentation site while `main` does not
explanation: §30.6 explains that a release packages a tagged commit as a stable, downloadable snapshot that does not change after the fact; this matters because if the sponsor pushes a bug fix mid-review, a reviewer looking at `main` would be reviewing a moving target, whereas a tagged release pins exactly what was reviewed and cited.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: Per §30.7, what does an "open-source license" legally accomplish when attached to a piece of code?
option_a: It automatically transfers copyright ownership to whoever downloads the code
option_b: It grants others specific permissions (e.g., to view, use, modify, redistribute) that copyright law would otherwise withhold by default -- code with no license attached carries no such permission, regardless of being publicly visible on GitHub
option_c: It guarantees the code has passed `devtools::check()` and all tests
option_d: It is required only for packages intended for commercial use
explanation: §30.7 states that without an explicit license, "the code is on GitHub" does not mean anyone has the legal right to reuse it -- silence is not permission. A license is a legal document granting permissions that copyright law would otherwise withhold.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: Per §30.7's distinction between permissive and copyleft licenses, what is the key practical consequence of licensing a package under the GPL family (copyleft) rather than MIT (permissive)?
option_a: GPL-licensed code cannot legally be used by anyone outside the original author's organisation
option_b: Any derivative work incorporating the GPL-licensed code must itself be released under the same copyleft license, so it cannot be quietly absorbed into a closed, proprietary product
option_c: GPL licensing automatically expires after five years, unlike MIT
option_d: MIT-licensed code requires payment of a royalty for commercial reuse, while GPL code does not
explanation: §30.7 explains that copyleft licenses (the GPL family) require any derivative work to be released under the same license -- "if you build on this, your building must stay open too" -- meaning copyleft code cannot be quietly absorbed into a closed, proprietary product, unlike permissively-licensed (MIT/Apache/BSD) code.

chapter: Chapter 30: R Packages and Pipelines
question: the ref-table from §30.7 comparing three common license choices (MIT License, GPL-3, CC-BY) across the columns "Commercial reuse allowed?", "Derivatives must stay open?", and "Typical use case". Based on this table, which license is described as typically used for written content, data, and reports rather than code?
option_a: MIT License
option_b: GPL-3
option_c: CC-BY
option_d: Apache 2.0
explanation: The §30.7 comparison table lists CC-BY as allowing commercial reuse with attribution, not requiring derivatives to stay open, with a typical use case of "written content, data, reports -- not typically used for code," distinguishing it from the code-oriented MIT and GPL-3 entries.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: What is a "reference case" in HTA methodology?
option_a: A legal contract between an agency and a manufacturer specifying price
option_b: An agency's defined "house style" for the base-case analysis -- a fixed set of choices (perspective, outcome measure, discount rate, time horizon) every submission must follow unless justified otherwise
option_c: A database of past appraisal decisions used only for audit purposes
option_d: A single numeric cost-effectiveness threshold published by the WHO
explanation: As defined in the difficult-terminology box in Section 31.1, a reference case is a fixed set of methodological choices that allows submissions from different companies and diseases to be compared on a like-for-like basis; scenario/sensitivity analyses may deviate from it, but the base case cannot without justification.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: What is Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, and why does it matter for HTAIn's work?
option_a: A private health insurance provider that commissions independent ERG critiques in India
option_b: India's DSU Technical Support Document series equivalent to NICE's TSDs
option_c: India's flagship public health insurance scheme providing cashless hospitalisation cover to lower-income households; HTAIn assessments feed into decisions about what its benefit package covers and at what reimbursement rate
option_d: A WHO-run threshold-setting committee for South Asian countries
explanation: Per Section 31.3's difficult-terminology box, PM-JAY is India's 2018-launched flagship public health insurance scheme, and it is the policy vehicle that HTAIn technology assessments ultimately feed into -- the Indian analogue of what a NICE guidance recommendation does for the NHS.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: How does the iDSI reference case for LMIC settings relate to an agency reference case like NICE's, and what is its most debated recommendation?
option_a: It is unrelated to the NICE concept; its main recommendation is a mandatory societal perspective
option_b: It is the same general concept (a standardised checklist of methodological choices so evaluations can be fairly compared) but aimed at countries without their own, and its most debated element is the willingness-to-pay threshold -- historically the 1-3x GDP-per-capita heuristic
option_c: It replaces QALYs with life-years as the only permitted outcome measure
option_d: It is a legally binding international treaty enforced by the WHO on all LMIC governments
explanation: Section 31.4's difficult-terminology box states a reference case is a standardised checklist (perspective, discount rate, uncertainty handling, comparators) so different models can be fairly compared, and that iDSI's version targets countries lacking their own; the chapter identifies the WTP threshold -- especially the now-deprecated 1-3x GDP-per-capita heuristic -- as its most consequential and debated recommendation.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: What is an Evidence Review Group (ERG) in the NICE Technology Appraisal process?
option_a: A NICE internal staff committee that sets the final GBP20,000-30,000/QALY threshold
option_b: The manufacturer's own in-house health economics team
option_c: An independent team, usually university-based health economists and clinicians (not NICE staff, not the manufacturer), commissioned to critically check a company's submitted model and evidence before the committee decides
option_d: A patient advocacy panel that votes on whether a drug should be reimbursed
explanation: Section 31.6's difficult-terminology box defines the ERG as an independent, usually academic team performing a structured, published peer review of the submitted cost-effectiveness model, with the company then given a formal chance to respond via technical engagement.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: Why is a "reference case" (as generically defined) distinct from the "Reference case (LMIC context)" discussion in Section 31.4, even though both boxes define the same underlying term?
option_a: The LMIC box redefines a reference case as a legally binding treaty rather than a methodological checklist
option_b: They describe the same core concept, but Section 31.4's box emphasizes that iDSI's reference case is specifically aimed at countries that do not yet have their own established one, unlike NICE's or CADTH's long-standing in-house versions
option_c: The generic reference case concept applies only to discount rates, while the LMIC version applies only to WTP thresholds
option_d: The LMIC reference case box states that iDSI's reference case overrides and replaces NICE's for any multinational submission
explanation: Both difficult-terminology boxes describe a reference case as a standardised methodological checklist enabling fair comparison across submissions; the distinguishing point raised in 31.4 is that the iDSI reference case exists precisely because many LMICs lack their own established reference case, unlike the mature NICE/CADTH versions covered earlier in the chapter.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: According to the Section 31.5 agency comparison table, which agency's approach deliberately avoids stating a cost-per-QALY threshold "by design" rather than simply omitting one?
option_a: NICE (UK)
option_b: PBAC (Australia)
option_c: IQWiG/G-BA (Germany)
option_d: ICER (USA)
explanation: The table and surrounding prose state IQWiG/G-BA uses an efficiency-frontier method with "no cost/QALY threshold by design" -- the chapter explicitly notes this is a considered methodological stance (tied to the AMNOG early benefit assessment process), not an omission.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: The Section 31.5 six-column agency comparison table (Agency, Perspective, Discount, WTP threshold, Comparator, Uncertainty) listing NICE, CADTH, PBAC, IQWiG/G-BA, HAS, ICER, and HTAIn. Based on this table, which agency's discount rate is explicitly listed as a fixed base-case percentage different from NICE's 3.5%?
option_a: CADTH -- "Per current guidance"
option_b: PBAC -- "5% base case"
option_c: HAS -- "Varies by guidance"
option_d: HTAIn -- "Per Indian guidance"
explanation: Among the table's entries, PBAC (Australia) is the one with an explicit fixed numeric discount rate stated in the table -- "5% base case" -- unlike CADTH, HAS, and HTAIn, whose discount conventions are described only qualitatively ("per current guidance," "varies by guidance," "per Indian guidance").

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: The chapter's R code example for an HTAIn-facing model parameterises a cost input across three scenarios: pmjay_tariff, public_tertiary, and private_estimate. What practical India-specific issue is this pattern designed to address?
option_a: The requirement to report results in both INR and USD simultaneously
option_b: The wide spread in unit costs for a given procedure across public, private, and PM-JAY empanelled-hospital tariffs, given sparser and more heterogeneous Indian cost data than UK/Canadian registries
option_c: A legal mandate that all HTAIn submissions must include exactly three discount rate scenarios
option_d: The need to convert QALYs into DALYs for every HTAIn submission
explanation: Section 31.3 explains that Indian unit costs vary substantially between public, private, and PM-JAY empanelled-hospital tariffs, and that data sparsity relative to NHS/CIHI registries pushes HTAIn-facing models toward treating data-source assumptions as a first-class sensitivity dimension -- illustrated by the unit_cost_scenarios code example.

chapter: Chapter 31: Agency Requirements and Reference Cases
question: According to Section 31.2, why can a model built strictly to NICE's reference case not simply be "relabeled" for a German IQWiG/G-BA submission under AMNOG?
option_a: Because Germany requires all models to be built in a different programming language than R
option_b: Because IQWiG's early benefit assessment is explicitly not a cost-effectiveness exercise -- it centres patient-relevant outcomes relative to a comparator and produces an additional-benefit rating that feeds into price negotiation, not an ICER-versus-threshold decision
option_c: Because Germany does not allow QALYs to be measured using the EQ-5D instrument
option_d: Because German law requires a 10% discount rate on all cost inputs
explanation: The chapter states that AMNOG's early benefit assessment centres patient-relevant outcomes and produces an "additional benefit" rating used in price negotiation rather than a cost-per-QALY decision, so a NICE-style QALY/ICER model needs substantial reworking -- not relabeling -- for a German submission.

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: According to Chapter 32, survival data are described as "immature" in an HTA submission when:
option_a: The trial Kaplan-Meier curve has flattened and reached its tail
option_b: A substantial fraction of patients have not yet died or progressed at the data cut, so the shape of the curve's tail is unknown and must be estimated
option_c: The sample size is too small for statistical significance
option_d: The trial used a single-arm design without a comparator
explanation: The chapter defines immature survival data as data where "a substantial fraction of patients in a trial have not yet died (or progressed) at the time of the data cut used for the HTA submission -- the Kaplan-Meier curve has not flattened out or reached its tail, so the shape of that tail is unknown and must be estimated rather than observed."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: A cure-fraction model in oncology survival extrapolation makes which structural assumption?
option_a: All patients eventually die according to a single parametric distribution
option_b: A proportion of the cohort -- the cure fraction -- experiences no excess disease-related mortality risk after some point, behaving thereafter like the general population
option_c: The hazard of death is constant across the entire follow-up period
option_d: Cure can only be modeled using a Weibull distribution
explanation: Per the chapter's difficult-terminology box, a cure-fraction model "explicitly assumes a proportion of the trial population -- the cure fraction -- will experience no excess risk of death from the disease once they pass some point, behaving thereafter like the general population... while the remaining patients continue to follow a standard survival distribution."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: What distinguishes a mixture cure model from a non-mixture cure model, per the chapter?
option_a: Mixture models require Bayesian priors; non-mixture models do not
option_b: A mixture model separates patients into two latent groups (cured vs. uncured, each following its own survival function); a non-mixture model instead rescales a single survival distribution so it asymptotes toward the cure proportion
option_c: Mixture models cannot be fitted using `flexsurvcure`
option_d: Non-mixture models always estimate a larger cure fraction than mixture models
explanation: The chapter states: "In a mixture cure model, the overall survival function is modelled as a weighted combination of two distinct groups... This contrasts with non-mixture cure models, which instead rescale a single survival distribution so it asymptotes towards the cure proportion as time extends, without separating patients into two latent groups."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: A plot showing the chapter's simulated single-arm oncology-style Kaplan-Meier survival curve with a plateau beginning near the end of the 60-month follow-up window, overlaid with two fitted curves -- a standard Weibull `flexsurvreg` fit (monotonic hazard) and a `flexsurvcure` mixture cure model fit (asymptoting toward the cure fraction) -- as produced by the chapter's R code. Based on that code, what was the simulated "true" cure fraction, and what does the fitted `theta` parameter represent?
option_a: true_cure_fraction = 0.50; theta is the Weibull shape parameter
option_b: true_cure_fraction = 0.30; theta is the estimated cure fraction, comparable against the simulated truth
option_c: true_cure_fraction = 0.30; theta is the median survival time
option_d: true_cure_fraction = 0.70; theta is the restricted mean survival time
explanation: The code sets `true_cure_fraction <- 0.30` and simulates ~30% of patients as administratively censored "cured" cases. The chapter notes: "The fitted 'theta' parameter is the estimated cure fraction, which can be compared against the simulated true_cure_fraction (0.30) as a sanity check."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: A single-arm trial, as defined in Chapter 32, is characterized by:
option_a: Patients randomized between the investigational treatment and placebo
option_b: All patients receiving the investigational treatment only, with effectiveness assessed against an external benchmark rather than a concurrent randomized comparator group
option_c: Two parallel non-randomized cohorts enrolled at different sites
option_d: A crossover design where each patient serves as their own control
explanation: Per the difficult-terminology box: "A single-arm trial enrolls patients onto the investigational treatment only, with no concurrent randomized comparator group... effectiveness is assessed against some external benchmark (historical data, a different trial, or a modelled natural-history estimate)."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: Per the chapter, the validity of a historical control comparison in ultra-rare disease HTA depends most critically on:
option_a: The historical dataset being larger than the trial's sample size
option_b: How similar the historical population truly is to the trial population in case-mix, era of care, and measurement
option_c: Whether the historical data was analysed using R rather than another statistical package
option_d: Using a Cox proportional hazards model instead of Kaplan-Meier estimation
explanation: The chapter states that historical controls' usefulness "is only as good as how similar the historical population truly is to the trial population in case-mix, era of care, and measurement -- differences that are easy to overlook and hard to fully correct for statistically."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: Why does Chapter 32 argue that a standard cohort Markov model tends to understate the benefit of a vaccination programme against a transmissible disease?
option_a: Markov models cannot incorporate discounting
option_b: Cohort Markov models treat transition probabilities as fixed inputs, with no mechanism for one simulated patient's vaccination status to alter another's risk, so they are blind to indirect (herd) protection
option_c: Markov models always assume 100% vaccine efficacy
option_d: Cohort models require a societal perspective that systematically overestimates programme costs
explanation: The chapter explains a cohort Markov model "has no mechanism for one simulated patient's vaccination status to alter another simulated patient's risk; it treats transition probabilities as fixed inputs... the standard cohort approach understates the benefit of vaccination... because it is blind to everyone who never gets infected simply because the people around them were vaccinated."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: According to Chapter 32, what distinguishes NICE's MTEP pathway from its DAP pathway?
option_a: MTEP evaluates drugs; DAP evaluates devices
option_b: MTEP generally uses cost-minimisation for technologies expected to be cost-saving or cost-neutral, while DAP applies full cost-effectiveness modelling for technologies expected to raise net cost in exchange for better outcomes
option_c: MTEP applies the £100,000/QALY HST threshold; DAP applies the standard threshold
option_d: DAP evaluates only vaccines while MTEP evaluates only gene therapies
explanation: Per the difficult-terminology box: "MTEP's use of cost-minimisation for technologies expected to be cost-saving or cost-neutral, against DAP's full cost-effectiveness modelling for technologies expected to raise net cost in exchange for better outcomes."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), as defined in the chapter, refers to:
option_a: Software embedded inside a physical hardware medical device
option_b: Software intended for a medical purpose that performs that purpose without being embedded in a physical device -- the software itself, running on general-purpose hardware, is the medical device
option_c: Any mobile health app regardless of its intended function
option_d: Software used only for hospital billing and administration
explanation: The chapter defines SaMD as software "intended to be used for a medical purpose... that performs that purpose without being embedded inside a physical hardware medical device -- the software itself, running on a general-purpose smartphone or server, *is* the medical device from a regulatory standpoint."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: Chapter 32 raises an unresolved regulatory/HTA question specific to AI-enabled SaMD. What is it?
option_a: Whether AI tools must always use a randomized comparator
option_b: Whether a retrained and updated model version is still "the same" technology originally evaluated, or requires re-evaluation as effectively a new product, given possible model drift/dataset shift
option_c: Whether AI software requires UKCA/CE marking at all
option_d: Whether the Evidence Standards Framework applies only to paediatric populations
explanation: The chapter asks: "if a vendor retrains the underlying model on new data and pushes an update, is that update still 'the same' technology that was originally evaluated, or does it need re-evaluation as effectively a new product?" -- noting regulators like MHRA and FDA are actively working through this via concepts like a "predetermined change control plan."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: "Durability (waning of effect)," in the context of one-time gene/cell therapies, refers to:
option_a: How quickly the drug is metabolized after infusion
option_b: How long the treatment's benefit persists once achieved, and the possibility that the benefit is not permanent -- patients may lose benefit over time through relapse or declining corrected gene expression
option_c: The time required for regulatory approval of the therapy
option_d: The budget impact of spreading payments over multiple years
explanation: Per the difficult-terminology box, durability "refers to how long a treatment's benefit persists once achieved, and 'waning of effect' describes the possibility that the benefit is not permanent -- that patients... may, at some point after treatment, begin losing that benefit, whether through biological relapse, loss of corrected gene expression over time, or simple regression toward the underlying disease's natural history."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: Per Chapter 32, which mechanism primarily reduces a payer's single-year budget shock from a one-time gene therapy's large upfront cost, rather than directly addressing durability-outcome uncertainty?
option_a: An outcomes-based refund triggered only by confirmed relapse
option_b: An annuity or staged-payment model spreading the single large payment over several years of instalments
option_c: A mixture cure model
option_d: The Evidence Standards Framework for Digital Health Technologies
explanation: The chapter describes annuity/staged-payment models as spreading "the single very large payment over several years of instalments... it does reduce the payer's single-year budget shock... and keeps some portion of each instalment contingent on evidence of continued benefit."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: The "cascade of care" framework, as applied to TB in Chapter 32, tracks patients through which sequence of steps?
option_a: Screening, insurance approval, discharge, follow-up
option_b: Diagnosis, treatment initiation, treatment completion, and cure -- with attrition possible at any step
option_c: Vaccination, infection, recovery, immunity
option_d: Enrollment, randomization, blinding, and analysis
explanation: The difficult-terminology box defines the cascade of care as tracking patients through "diagnosis... treatment initiation... treatment completion... and cure... attrition -- patients falling out of care -- can happen at *any* of these steps, not only at the final one."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: DOTS (directly observed treatment, short-course), as described in Chapter 32, is a WHO-promoted strategy whose core rationale is:
option_a: Reducing the cost of TB drugs through bulk procurement
option_b: Direct observation of each medication dose being swallowed, to assure adherence and reduce the risk of relapse and emergence of drug-resistant strains
option_c: Shortening TB treatment duration to under one month
option_d: Replacing sputum culture testing with chest X-ray screening
explanation: Per the chapter: "a healthcare worker... directly observes the patient swallowing each dose... because an incomplete TB treatment course both risks relapse for the individual patient and risks selecting for drug-resistant bacterial strains... direct observation was adopted as a core structural safeguard."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: The chapter's report-table "Illustrative TB cascade-of-care attrition for a hypothetical cohort of 10,000 presumptive TB cases," with columns for Cascade stage, Conditional probability, Cumulative probability, and Remaining (of 10,000), listing five stages: Presumptive TB, Diagnosed, Initiated treatment, Completed treatment, Bacteriologically cured. Based on this table, what is the cumulative probability and remaining cohort size at the final "Bacteriologically cured" stage?
option_a: Cumulative probability 0.700, remaining 7,000
option_b: Cumulative probability 0.595, remaining 5,950
option_c: Cumulative probability 0.428, remaining 4,284
option_d: Cumulative probability 0.476, remaining 4,760
explanation: The report-table's final row shows "Bacteriologically cured: Cond. prob. 0.90, Cum. prob. 0.428, Remaining 4,284" -- confirmed in the narrative text as "roughly 4,284 are ultimately confirmed cured -- a population-level cure rate of about 42.8%."

chapter: Chapter 32: Special Topics
question: Chapter 32 frames the health-system resource-allocation question (SS32.8) around which core economic concept?
option_a: A cost-effectiveness threshold represents an estimate of health forgone elsewhere in the system when money is spent on a new technology -- an opportunity cost -- applied explicitly across many competing claims on one fixed budget, as in a PBMA exercise
option_b: Cost-minimisation analysis should always be preferred over cost-utility analysis at the system level
option_c: Budget impact analysis entirely replaces the need for ICER thresholds
option_d: System-level allocation requires abandoning QALYs in favour of cost-per-life-year
explanation: The chapter states a cost-effectiveness threshold "is, properly understood, an estimate of the health forgone elsewhere in the system when money is spent on a new technology -- an *opportunity cost*... Zooming out... simply takes that same opportunity-cost logic and applies it explicitly across *many* competing claims on the same budget at once," citing programme budgeting and marginal analysis (PBMA) as the practical mechanism.

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: According to the chapter, what does Cronbach's alpha measure?
option_a: Whether a scale's items measure the "right" underlying construct
option_b: How closely a set of items on a scale move together across respondents (internal consistency)
option_c: The difficulty and discrimination parameters of individual items
option_d: Whether a hypothesised factor structure fits the observed response data
explanation: The chapter defines Cronbach's alpha as "a single number...summarising how closely a set of items on a scale move together across respondents," explicitly noting that "Alpha is not a measure of whether the items measure the *right* construct, only of whether they move together."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: What does confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) test, as described in the chapter?
option_a: Whether a pre-specified hypothesis about which items load onto which latent factor(s) is supported by the data
option_b: Whether individual items differ in difficulty and discrimination
option_c: Whether a scale's Cronbach's alpha exceeds 0.70
option_d: Whether stated preferences match revealed preferences
explanation: The chapter describes CFA as testing "a specific, pre-specified hypothesis about...structure," checking "how well real response data support that specific structure, rather than discovering a structure from scratch," likening it to "presenting a blueprint and asking 'does the building that was actually constructed match this blueprint?'"

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: In the chapter's `lavaan::cfa()` example fitting a two-factor model (`physical =~ p1 + p2 + p3`) to six simulated six-item Likert data, what does the `=~` operator mean in lavaan model syntax?
option_a: "is measured by" -- the latent factor on the left is measured by the observed items listed on the right
option_b: "is regressed on" -- the factor predicts the items as a linear regression
option_c: "is correlated with" -- specifies a covariance between the listed variables
option_d: "is equal to" -- constrains the items to identical numeric values
explanation: The chapter states: "Model structure is expressed with a compact formula syntax in which `=~` means 'is measured by' -- read `factor =~ item1 + item2 + item3` as 'this latent factor is measured by these observed items.'"

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: How does Item Response Theory (IRT) differ fundamentally from classical test theory (CTT), per the chapter?
option_a: IRT produces a single reliability number for the whole scale, exactly like CTT
option_b: IRT estimates difficulty and discrimination parameters for each item individually, rather than one reliability figure for the whole scale, underpinning computer-adaptive testing
option_c: IRT cannot support computer-adaptive testing because items must all be answered by every respondent
option_d: IRT requires fewer respondents and simpler statistics than CTT
explanation: The chapter notes "Unlike classical test theory, which produces one reliability number for the whole scale, IRT estimates parameters for each item individually," and that this "makes it statistically defensible for different patients to answer different subsets of items -- the basis of *computer-adaptive testing*."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: In the chapter's `mirt::mirt()` example modeling five binary mobility-limitation items with `itemtype = "2PL"`, what do the `a` and `d` outputs from `coef(irt_fit, simplify = TRUE)` represent?
option_a: "2PL" fits a one-parameter Rasch model; `coef()` returns only item difficulty
option_b: `a` is each item's discrimination parameter and `d` is its difficulty-related parameter, from a two-parameter logistic model
option_c: "2PL" is reserved for ordinal Likert items; `a` and `d` are standardised factor loadings
option_d: `a` and `d` are the estimated latent trait (theta) scores for each respondent
explanation: The chapter states the model uses `itemtype = "2PL"` for binary items "with both difficulty and discrimination parameters," and that "`coef()` returns the estimated discrimination (`a`) and difficulty-related (`d`) parameters for each item."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: As defined in the chapter, what is the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID)?
option_a: The smallest change in a score that is statistically significant at p < 0.05
option_b: The smallest change in a score that patients or clinicians would recognise as meaningful, as opposed to a change that is merely statistically detectable
option_c: The mean change observed in a placebo/control arm of a trial
option_d: The threshold above which a PRO instrument is considered fully validated
explanation: The chapter defines MCID as "the smallest change in a score...that patients or clinicians would recognise as meaningful, as opposed to a change that is merely detectable by a statistical test."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: What is the anchor-based method for estimating an MCID, per the chapter?
option_a: Taking half the baseline standard deviation of the scale as the threshold
option_b: Comparing PRO score change against an independent external indicator (e.g., a patient global rating of change), with the average score change among patients reporting a small-but-real improvement becoming the MCID estimate
option_c: Using the standard error of measurement derived from the instrument's reliability
option_d: Adopting a regulatory agency's fixed numerical threshold regardless of population
explanation: The chapter describes the anchor-based method as comparing "the change in a PRO score against an independent, external indicator ('anchor')," where "the average PRO score change among patients who selected 'a little better'...becomes the estimated MCID."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: The chapter describes the distribution-based method of estimating an MCID as relying on what?
option_a: Patient global ratings of change collected during follow-up visits
option_b: Qualitative interviews with clinicians about what matters most to patients
option_c: Statistical properties of the scale itself, such as half the baseline standard deviation (0.5 x SD) or the standard error of measurement, without needing additional patient input
option_d: A pre-registered clinical trial primary endpoint as the sole criterion
explanation: The chapter defines the distribution-based method as "using only the statistical properties of the scale itself -- most commonly a fraction of the scale's baseline standard deviation (half a standard deviation...) or the standard error of measurement," noting these "are quick to compute from existing trial data and need no additional patient input."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: A two-column academic report table titled "Illustrative responder analysis using a distribution-based MCID threshold (0.5 x baseline SD) on the simulated treatment-arm data," with rows "Baseline SD," "Distribution-based MCID (0.5 x SD)," "Mean observed change," and "Responder rate (change >= MCID)," plus a footer noting the data is illustrative/simulated. Based on the values shown in this table, what responder rate was reported?
explanation: The chapter's report table lists Baseline SD = 11.32 points, Distribution-based MCID (0.5 x SD) = 5.66 points, Mean observed change = 6.42 points, and Responder rate (change >= MCID) = 52.0%.

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: How does a mixed logit model (random-parameters logit) relax the key simplifying assumption of the standard conditional logit model used in DCE analysis, per the chapter?
option_a: It estimates a distribution of coefficients across the respondent population -- a mean effect plus a measure of person-to-person variation -- instead of one coefficient assumed identical for every respondent
option_b: It removes the need for an experimental design that systematically varies attribute levels
option_c: It assumes every respondent has identical risk tolerance for a given attribute
option_d: It replaces the type I extreme value (Gumbel) error assumption with a normal distribution for the systematic utility component
explanation: The chapter states mixed logit "relaxes the 'everyone has the same preferences' assumption of the standard conditional logit," estimating "a *distribution* of coefficients across the respondent population -- a mean effect plus a measure of how much that effect varies from person to person."

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: In the chapter's illustrative DCE dataset (`dce_long`), how must the data be structured before fitting `mlogit`, `apollo`, or `logitr`?
option_a: One row per respondent, with each attribute's chosen alternative stored as a separate column
option_b: One row per alternative, per choice task, per respondent, with a column per attribute and a `chosen` indicator (1 for the picked alternative, 0 for the rest)
option_c: One row per attribute, aggregated across all respondents and choice tasks
option_d: One row per choice task, recording only the winning alternative's attribute values
explanation: The chapter states the raw survey responses "have to be reshaped into the 'long' format that choice models expect: one row per alternative, per choice task, per respondent, with a column for each attribute and an indicator for whether that particular alternative was the one chosen," as shown in the `dce_long` example with `chosen` equal to 1 or 0.

chapter: Chapter 33: Patient-Reported Outcomes and Preference Research
question: What distinguishes best-worst scaling (BWS) from a plain rating-scale task, according to the chapter?
option_a: BWS asks respondents to rate every item independently on a 1-5 bothersomeness scale
option_b: BWS forces respondents to identify both the best and worst item/attribute-level in a shown set, revealing relative ranking information that plain rating scales (prone to ceiling effects) often fail to capture
option_c: BWS can only be applied to revealed-preference data, not stated-preference surveys
option_d: BWS removes any need for logit-family statistical models to analyse the resulting data
explanation: The chapter contrasts rating five symptoms (where several might all get rated "5") with BWS, where showing the same items and asking "which bothers you most, and which bothers you least...force[s] a direct comparison that reveals relative ranking information even when absolute intensities are similar," avoiding the "ceiling-effect or scale-use bias" that "plain rating scales are notoriously prone to."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: According to Section 34.1, how do machine learning methods such as random forests and gradient boosting fundamentally differ from the parametric and semiparametric methods used elsewhere in this book?
option_a: They require larger sample sizes before any model can be fit
option_b: They let the data determine the shape of the relationship rather than requiring the analyst to pre-specify a functional form in advance
option_c: They always produce more transparent, auditable results than parametric methods
option_d: They eliminate the need for a held-out test set
explanation: The chapter states that while prior methods require the analyst to "specify the functional form... before fitting it to data," ML methods "flip that order," letting "algorithms such as random forests and gradient boosting... let the data determine the shape of the relationship," at a real cost to interpretability and auditability.

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: In the chapter's worked example, `randomForest::randomForest()` is fit to simulated patient data to predict `high_cost_next_year`. What did the chapter report as the outcome of this run?
option_a: Roughly 78% test-set accuracy, with `n_comorbidities` and `prior_admissions` ranked as the strongest variable-importance predictors
option_b: Roughly 95% test-set accuracy, with `age` as the sole important predictor
option_c: Roughly 50% test-set accuracy, indicating the model failed to learn any signal
option_d: Roughly 78% test-set accuracy, with `baseline_cost` and `age` ranked as the top predictors
explanation: The text reports "the forest achieves roughly 78% accuracy on the held-out test set, and the variable-importance output ranks `n_comorbidities` and `prior_admissions` as the strongest predictors," matching clinical intuition about repeat high-cost patients.

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Why does the chapter's pitfall box caution that variable importance and SHAP values do not make a random forest an acceptable replacement for a transparent decision-analytic model in most HTA submissions?
option_a: Because `randomForest::importance()` cannot be computed in R without `caret`
option_b: Because these measures are approximations layered on top of the black box after the fact, not the underlying structure itself, so an ensemble of hundreds of trees still has no equivalent to a Markov model's transition table that a reviewer can trace by hand
option_c: Because variable importance always contradicts clinical intuition and therefore cannot be trusted
option_d: Because HTA bodies formally prohibit any model with test accuracy above 80%
explanation: The pitfall box states that variable importance plots and SHAP values "genuinely help explain what the model is doing, but they are an approximation layered on top of the black box after the fact, not the box itself -- they do not make the underlying ensemble of hundreds of trees auditable in the way a transparent state-transition structure is."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Per Section 34.2, which three tasks does the chapter identify as the current, genuine pilot uses of large language models in HEOR workflows?
option_a: SLR screening triage, structured data extraction from published reports, and coding assistance for R-based HEOR models
option_b: Replacing dual-reviewer screening entirely, writing final submission conclusions, and setting discount rates
option_c: Running Markov cohort simulations unsupervised and generating input parameters without review
option_d: Conducting automated negotiations with HTA agencies
explanation: The chapter lists "three uses... common enough to be worth covering honestly": SLR screening assistance (triage, not decision), structured data extraction from published reports, and coding assistance for R-based HEOR models.

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Per the chapter's difficult-terminology box, what is a "hallucination" in the context of LLM use?
option_a: The model refusing to generate output whenever it is uncertain
option_b: A fluent, confident, plausible-sounding statement that is factually wrong or entirely fabricated, with no signal in the output distinguishing it from a correct statement
option_c: A visual artifact that only occurs when an LLM processes images
option_d: An error message produced only when the model exceeds its context window
explanation: The box defines hallucination as the model "generating a statement that is fluent, confident, and plausible-sounding, but factually wrong or entirely fabricated, with no signal in the model's output to distinguish it from a correct statement."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Per Section 34.3, what genuinely distinguishes an ambitious health-care "digital twin" claim from the microsimulation and DES models already built elsewhere in this book?
option_a: The use of Markov transition probabilities instead of individual trajectories
option_b: Mainly the data pipeline -- a digital twin aspires to be calibrated continuously or near-continuously to a specific patient's real-world data stream, rather than the underlying simulation algorithm
option_c: Digital twins exclusively use discrete-event simulation engines
option_d: Digital twins involve no simulated patients at all
explanation: The chapter states that "what distinguishes the more ambitious 'digital twin' framings... is less the modelling algorithm and more the *data pipeline* feeding it," since a true digital twin aims to be "calibrated, continuously or near-continuously, to a specific patient's real-world data stream."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Per Section 34.3's pitfall box, why can synthetic data not substitute for real patient-level evidence in an HTA submission?
option_a: It is prohibitively expensive to generate compared with real data collection
option_b: It preserves the source data's statistical patterns but carries no independent evidentiary status of its own, and a generative model fitted to biased or erroneous real data can "launder" those flaws into output that looks clean
option_c: Regulators have legally banned the use of synthetic data in any health context
option_d: Synthetic data always requires more computing power than the original analysis
explanation: The pitfall box states synthetic data "must never be presented to a reimbursement agency as if it carries the same evidential weight as the real IPD... synthetic data has no independent evidentiary status of its own," and the surrounding text warns a generative model can reproduce the source data's "bias or error... often without any visible warning sign."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Per Section 34.4, what is the stated general mission of ISPOR's Open-Source Models Special Interest Group?
option_a: To mandate that all HTA submissions be built exclusively in Excel
option_b: To promote the development, use, and transparent review of open-source health-economic models, including those built in R, as a counterpoint to closed, proprietary modelling environments
option_c: To formally certify individual R packages before they are accepted onto CRAN
option_d: To replace the R Consortium as the primary funder of core R infrastructure
explanation: The chapter describes the SIG's "general mission" as promoting "the development, use, and transparent review of health-economic models built in open-source tools, including R, as a counterpoint to the historically dominant closed, proprietary modelling environments."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Per the chapter's difficult-terminology box in Section 34.5, how is a "living systematic review" defined?
option_a: A review repeated completely from scratch on a fixed multi-year schedule
option_b: A systematic review maintained as an ongoing process, where new studies are continuously or on a short regular cycle searched for, screened, and incorporated, rather than being redone from scratch only periodically
option_c: A review conducted entirely by an LLM with no human screening step
option_d: A meta-analysis restricted to surviving (not deceased) trial participants
explanation: The box defines it as "a systematic review that is maintained as an ongoing process rather than a one-off project -- new studies are continuously (or on a short, regular cycle) searched for, screened, and incorporated... rather than the review being redone from scratch only every few years."

chapter: Chapter 34: Emerging Methods and the Future of HEOR in R
question: Which of the following is explicitly contradicted by the chapter's discussion of the obstacles currently limiting living economic models to an aspiration rather than standard HTA practice?
option_a: There is an open governance question about who approves an updated model and what threshold of change should trigger formal agency re-review
option_b: The computational cost of re-running the model is, by itself, the single largest and most underestimated burden of a living model
option_c: Genuinely continuous updating requires sustained data-pipeline maintenance, monitoring for upstream data changes, and ongoing analyst time
option_d: A defensible, version-controlled audit trail tying each submitted number to the specific model version that produced it becomes a structural requirement, not a nice-to-have
explanation: The chapter explicitly states the opposite: "the computational re-run itself is often the cheapest part of the exercise" -- the real maintenance burden is sustained data-pipeline upkeep and analyst time, not compute cost, while governance and versioning/audit-trail gaps are both named as genuine unresolved obstacles.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: Per the chapter's difficult-terminology box, what is a "frailty" term in the Case Study C microsimulation?
option_a: A measure of how physically weak an elderly patient is, used only for patients over 80
option_b: An unobserved, patient-specific multiplier applied to a baseline hazard or risk, drawn once per patient and applied to every relevant transition for that patient's entire simulated life, to represent heterogeneity not explained by other variables in the model
option_c: A random number redrawn every cycle to add short-term noise to each patient's risk
option_d: The probability that a patient drops out of the microsimulation before the horizon ends
explanation: The chapter defines a frailty as "an unobserved, patient-specific multiplier applied to a baseline hazard or risk to represent heterogeneity that isn't explained by the variables in the model," noting that drawing one frailty value per patient (not re-drawn each cycle) is what creates lasting high-risk and low-risk subgroups within the cohort.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: In Case Study A's base-case Markov model CEA (CKD add-on therapy vs standard of care), what was the deterministic ICER?
option_a: 1,559 per QALY
option_b: 44,941 per QALY
option_c: 28,829 per QALY
option_d: 103,339 per QALY
explanation: The chapter's report-table shows an incremental cost of 44,941 and an incremental QALY of 1.559 over the 25-year horizon, giving a deterministic base-case ICER of 44,941 / 1.559 = 28,829 per QALY.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: In Case Study B, where do the OS hazard ratio (0.68) and PFS hazard ratio (0.74) applied to the new agent's survival curves come from?
option_a: They are fitted directly from the comparator arm's own patient-level data using flexsurv
option_b: They are treated as already-validated outputs of a network meta-analysis (as covered conceptually in Chapter 12), taken as fixed inputs to project the new agent's curves from the comparator's fitted curves
option_c: They are assumed equal to 1.0 and then adjusted downward by expert judgement
option_d: They are estimated by comparing the new agent against platinum-based chemotherapy in a real head-to-head trial
explanation: The case study explicitly states that no head-to-head trial exists against every comparator, so an NMA has "already been run elsewhere" to produce the OS and PFS hazard ratios; the case study takes these as fixed, already-validated inputs rather than re-deriving the NMA itself.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: Across Case Study B's three structural-uncertainty scenarios (Weibull base case, log-logistic OS extrapolation, and OS benefit waning months 24-36), which statement correctly describes how the ICER moves?
option_a: The ICER is identical across all three scenarios, since the hazard ratios are held fixed
option_b: The log-logistic extrapolation produces the highest ICER (448,345), the waning scenario produces an ICER closer to the Weibull base case (341,219) than to the log-logistic scenario, and the ICER moves by roughly 40% across the full range
option_c: The waning scenario produces the highest ICER, because waning always makes a treatment look worse than an alternative extrapolation choice
option_d: The base case has the highest ICER, since the log-logistic and waning scenarios both allow the new agent's benefit to persist indefinitely
explanation: The chapter reports Weibull base case 321,271, log-logistic extrapolation 448,345 (highest), and waning 341,219 (closer to the Weibull base case than to the log-logistic scenario) -- because waning only erodes the benefit in years 2-3, while the log-logistic fit flattens the entire comparator tail. The chapter notes the ICER "moves by roughly 40% across the three scenarios."

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: Case Study C's base-case result for the colorectal cancer screening microsimulation showed a negative incremental cost (-655.33) and a positive incremental QALY (+0.5050). How does the chapter say this result should be reported?
option_a: As a standard ICER of -1,297.69 per QALY, interpreted literally as "screening saves 1,297.69 per QALY lost"
option_b: As a "dominant" strategy -- screening is both cheaper and more effective, so the usual accept/reject-against-a-threshold logic does not apply, and the negative ratio should not be read as a literal cost-per-QALY figure
option_c: As an inconclusive result requiring a larger cohort before any interpretation is possible
option_d: As a "dominated" strategy, since a negative number in a CEA conventionally signals the comparator is preferred
explanation: The chapter's heor-practice box states explicitly that a negative incremental cost paired with a positive incremental QALY means the strategy is "dominant," and that the arithmetic ratio should be labelled as such rather than reported as a bare cost-per-QALY number, since the same negative ratio could otherwise arise from the opposite (dominated) situation.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: In Case Study C's two-layer PSA, what distinguished the "first-order-only" ICER draws from the "second-order" ICER draws, and what did the comparison show?
option_a: First-order draws held all parameters fixed and only varied the patient-level random seed; second-order draws additionally resampled four structural parameters each draw. The second-order standard deviation was 2.32 times the first-order standard deviation, though all draws still showed screening as dominant
option_b: First-order draws used a smaller cohort size than second-order draws, so the difference was purely due to sample size
option_c: First-order and second-order draws produced identical spreads, confirming that parameter uncertainty does not matter once the cohort is large enough
option_d: Second-order draws removed patient-level stochastic noise entirely, leaving only parameter uncertainty
explanation: The chapter runs 40 draws of each configuration: first-order-only varies just the random seed with parameters fixed (sd 214.8), while second-order additionally resamples sensitivity, presentation probability, treatment cost, and death hazard (sd 498.7) -- a ratio of 2.32. Every one of the 40 second-order draws still showed screening as cost-saving and QALY-gaining.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: In Case Study D's 5-year budget impact analysis for a long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotic, what happened to the net budget impact as a percentage of reference spend between year 1 and year 5?
option_a: It stayed roughly constant at 13.9% throughout
option_b: It fell from 22.9% in year 1 to 3.4% in year 5
option_c: It rose from roughly 3.4% in year 1 to roughly 22.9% in year 5, as uptake of the new LAI increased
option_d: It was negative in year 1 (cost-saving) before turning positive in later years
explanation: The chapter's year-by-year table shows the net budget impact rising from 3.4% of reference spend in 2026 to 22.9% by 2030, tracking the uptake ramp from 4% to 27% of the eligible population, since the LAI's higher per-patient cost outweighs its relapse-cost offset at every point across the horizon.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: In Case Study E's propensity-score analysis (SGLT2i add-on vs standard intensification in type 2 diabetes), how did the naive unadjusted treatment-effect estimate compare to the matched and weighted estimates, relative to the true simulated effect of -0.55 percentage points?
option_a: The naive estimate (-0.473) was closer to the true effect than either the matched (-0.504) or weighted (-0.490) estimates
option_b: The naive estimate (-0.473) was further from the true effect than both the matched (-0.504) and weighted (-0.490) estimates, which both recovered the true effect more closely after propensity-score adjustment
option_c: All three estimates (naive, matched, weighted) were identical, since the confounders were fully measured
option_d: The matched estimate was further from the truth than the naive estimate, showing that matching introduced bias
explanation: The naive comparison returned -0.473, while the matched estimate (-0.504, 95% CI -0.599 to -0.409) and the weighted estimate (-0.490, 95% CI -0.555 to -0.426) both landed closer to the true simulated effect of -0.55, with both confidence intervals including the true value -- demonstrating that propensity-score adjustment reduced the confounding bias present in the naive comparison.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: In Case Study F's TB active case-finding (ACF) cascade-of-care analysis for an LMIC setting, how did adding ACF to standard of care (SOC) change the number of patients completing treatment, out of 600 total active TB cases in the cohort?
option_a: Completions fell from 298 (SOC) to 186 (SOC + ACF), because ACF diverted resources away from passive case detection
option_b: Completions rose from 186 (SOC alone) to 298 (SOC + ACF), an increase of 113 additional patients completing a full course of treatment
option_c: Completions stayed at 186 in both arms, since ACF only affects diagnosis, not treatment completion
option_d: All 600 active cases completed treatment once ACF was added, since ACF screens the entire non-presenting population
explanation: The chapter states that of 600 active TB cases, only 186 complete treatment under SOC alone (most loss occurring before diagnosis), while adding ACF -- which screens 189 of the 270 non-presenting cases -- lifts total completions to 298, a gain of 113 additional completers.

chapter: Chapter 35: End-to-End Worked Case Studies
question: Why does Case Study F deliberately avoid stating a specific country's official cost-effectiveness threshold figure when interpreting its ICER of roughly 52.5 LCU per DALY averted?
option_a: Because LMIC settings never use cost-effectiveness thresholds at all
option_b: Because inventing a specific country's official threshold would misrepresent a genuine, contested, country-specific policy parameter as a settled number; the chapter instead describes the general principle (per Chapter 31 SS31.4) that locally-derived thresholds, grounded in a health system's own budget constraints, are now considered more defensible than an imported "1-3x GDP per capita" rule of thumb
option_c: Because the ICER of 52.5 LCU per DALY averted is too small to be meaningfully compared against any threshold
option_d: Because DALYs cannot be compared against a monetary threshold, only QALYs can
explanation: The chapter explains that the older "1-3x GDP per capita" convention is now generally regarded as too permissive and poorly grounded in actual opportunity cost, and that more defensible approaches (the iDSI reference-case approach, referenced back to Chapter 31 SS31.4) derive thresholds locally from the health system's own budget and forgone health gains -- so stating a specific invented country figure would misrepresent a real, contested policy parameter.
